TODDLER 1 · LESSON 7

First Words: Food & Home for Toddlers 12–18 Months

Age 12–18 MonthsSubject Talk & ThinkClass Toddler 1Duration 3–5 minutes

Between twelve and eighteen months, toddlers point at everything, understand far more than they can say and love hearing you name their world. This class pairs eleven everyday pictures — an apple, a banana, an orange, a cup of milk, bread, an egg, then a cup, a spoon, a shoe, a sock and a chair — shown one at a time while you say the word simply and clearly.

There is no script and nothing to test. You name it, your toddler looks, points or has a go in their own way, and every calm repetition — apple, cup, shoe, chair — feeds those growing first words. Short, playful sessions of three to five minutes are all it takes.

Start Today’s Class ↓Eleven cards, one at a time. Name it, pause, and let your toddler answer in their own way.

PARENT INSTRUCTIONS

How to use this activity

Show one picture at a time and clearly name what you see. Keep your words short and natural: ‘apple’, ‘banana’, ‘shoe’ or ‘This is your cup.’

Pause after saying the word and give your toddler time to look, point, gesture, make a sound or respond in their own way.

When possible, connect the picture with the real object. If you show the spoon card, find a spoon at home and name it again.

There is no need to test your toddler or require them to repeat every word.

Every child develops differently. Kiddo School age ranges are guides, not tests or developmental deadlines.

TRY TOGETHER

Little things to say.

Prompts for you, not for the cards — say them softly while your baby looks.

  • Apple. This is an apple.
  • Banana. Yum!
  • Here is your cup.
  • Spoon.
  • Where is your shoe?
  • Sock. Peek-a-boo toes.
REAL-WORLD CONNECTION

Find It at Home

Turn the flashcards into a real-world activity. After looking at a card, find the same object around your home when appropriate.

  • Spoon → find a spoon.
  • Cup → find your toddler’s cup.
  • Shoe → find a shoe.
  • Sock → find a sock.
  • Chair → point to a chair.
  • Orange → find an orange in the fruit bowl.

    Apple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The food cards begin with the most familiar fruit in the house. This lesson pairs the card with the real apple — taste plus word — and shows how to answer the attempts that come back.

    What is this?

    An apple is a round fruit your toddler has likely already held, gummed and hurled off the high chair — the word arrives with history. The card shows a red apple; the fruit bowl supplies the moving, edible version.

    What does it mean?

    First words attach best to things a child can hold, taste and demand. The apple has all three: snack-sized, familiar and genuinely wanted, which makes it one of the highest-probability first food words in any kitchen.

    What does the child need to know?

    Show the card at real snack time and pair it with a real slice — word, taste, word. When an attempt comes back ("ah!", "pah!"), answer as if the word were perfect: "Yes! Apple!" Attempts that get answered become words; attempts that get ignored become silence.

    Why this matters

    Food words are daily words: they carry real wants, which gives your toddler a reason to say them. Every rehearsed "apple" at the fruit bowl is language doing actual work — and work is what makes words stick.

    What it teaches

    First food vocabulary, word attempts and pronunciation shaping, matching picture to object, and the wanting-asking-getting loop that powers early speech.

    Words to learn

    appleredbiteyumfruitmore

    Say this to your child

    “"Apple! A big red apple. Here is the picture apple, and here is your apple, waiting. Bite, bite — yum, yum. Red and round and sweet. All gone, apple — more tomorrow."”

    Step by step

    1. Set the card beside your toddler’s snack, not across the table: "Apple. This is an apple."
    2. Hand over a slice of real apple while repeating the word, so the taste and the name land together.
    3. Point at the card’s apple, then the real one, then back: same word, two apples. Matching play is the game this age plays best.
    4. Wait three full seconds after each naming — the pause is where attempts live. Whatever sound returns, answer it warmly: "Yes! Apple!"
    5. Finish with the last bite: "All gone apple!" Endings are words too, and this one gets a smile every time.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a red apple, drawn large and plain — the opener of the food cards. Say exactly that much; the richer show is at the table, where the card apple sits beside the real one and a small hand decides which is for eating.

    Ask your child

    Watch the attempts across the week: does "ah" become "bah", does the word arrive at the fruit bowl unprompted? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which consonant you are cooking up in there."

    What your child can say or do

    A first "ba" or "ah-poo" aimed at the fruit, the card apple matched to the real one with a proud tap, both arms wrapping a whole apple and walking off with it, or the word "apple" delivered at breakfast out of nowhere — spontaneous naming is the milestone of this whole stage.

    Out in the real world

    Apples fill the week: the fruit bowl, the slices at snack, the sauce at dinner, the pile at the shop. Every one is a replay — one clear word, one real apple, and the vocabulary grows where the appetite is.

    Try it together

    Apple hunt: hide the card and one real apple in easy spots and let your toddler find and match them. Finding, carrying, matching and naming is a full circuit — and the pride at the end is the best part.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did you answer every attempt as if it were the word, and did the card meet the real apple at least once? Warm replies and matching are the two halves; both are yours to give.

    Parent tips

    Offer, never demand — no "say apple" drills. The word is yours to provide and theirs to take. If your toddler says the word and then throws the apple, fine: naming and physics are separate subjects, and both are being studied.

    Staying safe

    Apple is a chewing challenge at this age: serve thin slices or soft-cooked pieces, seat your toddler upright and stay close through the snack — whole apples and big rounds belong to older teeth. Keep whole grapes and nuts off the menu entirely.

    This lesson pairs with the Apple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    Banana — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Banana arrives with a ritual attached: the peel. This lesson turns that ceremony into the lesson itself — word at the peel, word at the bite, and a warm answer for whatever version comes back.

    What is this?

    A banana is a soft yellow fruit that opens in strips — one of the few foods with a built-in unveiling. The card shows a yellow banana; the real one provides the slow reveal that keeps your toddler watching.

    What does it mean?

    The peel is the magic trick: your toddler watches the banana open, wants what is inside, and suddenly has a reason to say the word. Words tied to wanting and watching outperform words tied to mere showing — the banana is engineering in your favour.

    What does the child need to know?

    Say the word at the moment of peak interest — mid-peel: "banana". Then again at the bite. Whatever comes back — "nana", "ba", a shout — answer warmly and hand over the goods. The word is the ticket; the banana is the ride.

    Why this matters

    Banana attempts often arrive early because the word is fun to shape and the reward is instant. Early attempts deserve the same reply as clear words: every answered try keeps the talking pipeline open, and the pipeline matters more than the pronunciation.

    What it teaches

    Word attempts and shaping, the peeling sequence as vocabulary context, self-feeding, and the anticipation-reply loop that keeps first words coming.

    Words to learn

    bananapeelyellowsoftnanayum

    Say this to your child

    “"Banana! A yellow banana, soft and sweet. Watch — the peel comes down, strip by strip. Here is your piece, nana. Bite, bite, yum. All gone — the banana is finished, only the peel is left, bye-bye banana."”

    Step by step

    1. Bring the card and the banana together: "Banana. A yellow banana — here is the picture, here is the fruit."
    2. Start the peel slowly and say the word at the first strip: "Banana." Let the opening do the teaching.
    3. Offer a piece as you name it again, and let your toddler hold their own piece — holding and naming belong together now.
    4. Wait through the silence after each naming; answer every attempt — "nana!" — with the full word back, warmly: "Yes! Banana!"
    5. Close with the empty skin: "All gone!" — and let your toddler wave the peel goodbye if they wish. Ceremonies end; that is what makes them ceremonies.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a yellow banana, plain and clear on the card. Name it, then run the real unveiling at the table — the card shows the fruit, and the peel supplies the drama the picture cannot.

    Ask your child

    Watch the peel: do the eyes lock at the first strip, does the word or its baby version arrive mid-ceremony? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if the peel is the reason this word is coming early."

    What your child can say or do

    A proud "nana" at the counter, the whole word attempted and landing as "ba-ba", both fists on the peel helping it open, or the banana carried to the card for a matching tap — first words, naming and matching play, all in one snack.

    Out in the real world

    Bananas hang around: the fruit bowl, the shop, the lunchbox, the mash in the porridge. Each appearance takes one word — and this word, said constantly by toddlers everywhere, tends to stick like few others.

    Try it together

    Peel-it-myself: start the tear with a thumbnail, then give the banana to your toddler to open. The triumph of the first self-peeled banana is enormous, and the word rides on the triumph.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word land at the peel and at the bite, and did every attempt get a warm answer within a second or two? Fast, warm replies are the fuel this stage runs on.

    Parent tips

    Accept every version — "nana" is the word wearing training wheels, and correcting it only slows the wheels. If your toddler goes off bananas for a week, park the card; appetite returns, and the word waits patiently.

    Staying safe

    Mash or slice for new chewers and stay within reach at snack time — soft round pieces still need watching. Banana is among the gentler first fruits, but every food at this age is eaten sitting down, with a grown-up nearby.

    This lesson pairs with the Banana flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    Orange — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The orange card carries a quiet double: a fruit and a colour sharing one name. This lesson keeps it simple — peel, smell, name — and lets the double meaning sort itself out later.

    What is this?

    An orange is a round citrus fruit with a thick peel and a smell that fills the room when it opens. The card shows a bright orange; the word names the fruit and, handily, the colour — two ideas riding on one name.

    What does it mean?

    Toddlers do not need the fruit-colour split explained; hearing "orange" for both quietly builds two folders under one label, and the folders separate on their own later. Meanwhile the smell gives the word a second sense to anchor to.

    What does the child need to know?

    Peel the real orange at the table and say the word into the released smell: "orange". Smell plus sight plus taste makes a three-sense word, and three-sense words are the stickiest kind. Skip the explanation of the double name entirely.

    Why this matters

    Multi-sensory words — seen, smelled, tasted — collect more memory hooks than any flashcard can offer on its own. The orange is the set’s best example: the peel’s tear, the citrus smell and the bright round fruit all point at the same name.

    What it teaches

    Multi-sensory vocabulary, smell as a learning channel, the fruit-colour overlap left to sort itself, and naming through everyday kitchen routines.

    Words to learn

    orangepeelsmellroundjuicypieces

    Say this to your child

    “"Orange! A big round orange. Peel, peel — hear it open? Smell that — mmm, orange. Here is a piece, juicy and sweet. Orange for eating today — and orange is a colour too, but mostly orange is for yum."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card with the real orange beside it: "Orange. Here is an orange."
    2. Start the peel and pause at the first scent — say the word into the smell: "Orange. Mmm, smell that."
    3. Hold the fruit near — not under — your toddler’s nose and let them breathe it in; some lean in, some wrinkle their nose, and both are data.
    4. Hand over a piece and name it once more: "Orange. Yum." Then let the eating happen; the word has already landed three times.
    5. Finish by offering the empty peel for a last sniff — the ending of the ceremony is part of the ceremony.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a bright, round orange, plain on the card. Say that much, then bring the real fruit forward — the card cannot send the smell across the table, and the smell does half the teaching.

    Ask your child

    Watch the sniff: does your toddler lean in or pull back, and does the word get tried at the smell or the taste? Wonder aloud: "I wonder which sense is doing the heavy lifting for you."

    What your child can say or do

    A leaned-in sniff and a delighted "mmm", the word attempted at the peel — "oh-oh" is a fine start — the card orange tapped against the real one, or "orange" said at the fruit bowl a day later, out of nowhere, on purpose.

    Out in the real world

    Oranges appear all winter: the bowl, the segments at snack, the shop displays, the smell of one opened in another room. The nose finds them first — and the word follows the nose.

    Try it together

    Smell test: line up an orange, a banana and a bread roll, sniff each in turn and name it. A three-item smell-and-name is a complete sensory game, and the orange wins it on drama every time.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word ride the smell at least once, and did you resist explaining the double name? Simple naming now, sorting later — the order matters.

    Parent tips

    If the peel frustrates your toddler, start the tear and hand it over — shared ceremonies stay fun. The colour meaning needs nothing from you at all; saying "orange" at the fruit and at an orange toy does the whole job quietly.

    Staying safe

    Peel fully — pith and skin are chewy and bitter — and cut rounds into pieces for new chewers. Stay close through citrus snacks, and keep the card clear of the juice: paper and orange part badly.

    This lesson pairs with the Orange flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    Milk cup — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Milk is the centre of the day, and the cup that holds it is this set’s grammar lesson in disguise: two words, one thing. This lesson names the ritual your toddler would happily run anyway.

    What is this?

    A milk cup is the cup that brings the milk — at 12–18 months possibly the most sought object in the home. The card shows a cup of milk; the name is two words, which makes it your toddler’s first taste of how words combine.

    What does it mean?

    Two-word names are grammar seeds: hearing "milk cup" teaches that small words can join to make a bigger idea. Months before your toddler builds a first sentence, they are hearing the technique demonstrated on the thing they want most.

    What does the child need to know?

    Show the card just before the milk moment and say the whole name: "Milk cup. Your milk is coming." The routine teaches the word almost by itself — your job is the pairing and the pause, not the repetition.

    Why this matters

    Ritual words arrive early because they come with perfect timing, built-in motivation and daily rehearsal. A named milk cup also gives your toddler a route to requesting — understanding the name is the first step towards asking for it, which is power they will use.

    What it teaches

    Two-word comprehension, routine vocabulary, requesting (reaching, pointing, soon words), and sequence learning — cup, milk, sit, drink, finished.

    Words to learn

    milkcupdrinkmorepleasefinished

    Say this to your child

    “"Milk cup! The milk cup card. Here it comes — your very own milk cup. Milk, then cup: milk cup. Sit down, drink up, sip by sip. All gone — finished! The milk cup goes back to the kitchen until next time."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card just before milk time, while the wanting is visible: "Milk cup! Here comes the milk cup."
    2. Say both words slowly and let the cup arrive: "Milk... cup." The pause between them is your toddler’s first compound word, served in two parts.
    3. Hand the cup over and name the drink quietly once: "Drink your milk." No commentary track; the ritual is running.
    4. When the cup is empty, close the scene: "All gone! Finished." The ending word is as useful as the name, and easier to feel.
    5. Later in the week, hold up the card at an odd moment and watch: a word, a sound or a beeline for the kitchen means the name has moved in.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a cup of milk, plain and unmistakable. Name it, then step back — the real ceremony at your kitchen table is the fuller production, and your toddler is its director.

    Ask your child

    Watch the routine across the week: does the word, a sound or a beeline to the kitchen arrive when the card appears? Wonder aloud: "I wonder when the name and the want became the same thing for you."

    What your child can say or do

    A beeline for the high chair at the words "milk cup", both hands out and opening, the word "milk" or "mah" delivered at the cupboard, or the card carried to you as an order form — using a symbol to request is the biggest kind of news.

    Out in the real world

    The milk cup runs the day: morning, after the park, before bed. Each ritual is a full replay — the name before, one quiet word during, "finished" at the end. Three words a day, and every one of them does work.

    Try it together

    Doll’s milk time: pour pretend milk for a teddy, name the teddy’s milk cup, and let your toddler do the pouring. Pretend versions of rituals are how this age rehearses the words that matter most.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the name arrive before the cup rather than after, and did the ritual stay calm, un-narrated to death? Timing and restraint — the two skills this card quietly teaches you.

    Parent tips

    Two words said as one name — resist sliding into long sentences; "milk cup" is the whole payload. If your toddler calls every cup "milk cup", that is normal sorting-in-progress, and the folders fix themselves with time.

    Staying safe

    Check warm milk at your wrist before serving, keep drinking seated, and keep the card out of the ritual’s splash zone — paper and milk part badly. Cots stay card-free, milk or no milk.

    This lesson pairs with the Milk cup flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    Bread — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Bread is a comfort word: soft, daily and nearly always on the table. This lesson names it where it lives — the kitchen — and lets your toddler’s hands do the remembering.

    What is this?

    Bread is the soft baked staple at most meals — toast at breakfast, sandwiches at lunch, the crust handed over from your plate. The card shows a loaf; the kitchen supplies the real thing several times a day.

    What does it mean?

    The kitchen is where toddlers gravitate anyway — noise, grown-ups, food — so words learned there collect rehearsals all day long. Naming bread, and the foods beside it, turns a place your toddler loves into the vocabulary room it already is.

    What does the child need to know?

    Hand over the word with the texture: "Bread. Soft bread." Let your toddler squish a piece — squish counts as research at this age — and name it once at the giving. Texture words arrive free with food words; collect them quietly.

    Why this matters

    Food words are requested words: they carry wants, which is the strongest engine a first word can have. Bread also travels — the shop, grandma’s house, the café — so the word gets rehearsed far beyond your kitchen.

    What it teaches

    Food vocabulary through texture and taste, kitchen routine words, sensory language (soft, warm, crusty), and the requesting loop that keeps first words working.

    Words to learn

    breadsoftcrusttoastcrumbyum

    Say this to your child

    “"Bread! A loaf of bread, soft and lovely. Here is your piece — feel it, soft, soft. Bite, bite, yum. The crust is crunchy, the middle is soft. Bread at breakfast, bread at lunch — bread is a friend of ours."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at a bread moment — while the sandwich is being made, not after the plate is cleared: "Bread. This is bread."
    2. Offer a piece and name it at the handover: "Bread for you. Soft." The word arrives with the texture already in the fingers.
    3. Let one honest squish happen — a full experiment — then name it once more: "Bread. Squeezy."
    4. Point at the card’s loaf, then the real bread, then back: same word, two loaves. Matching play does the rest.
    5. Keep the crust for the finale — "crust! the bread’s coat" — or let it be the dog’s, but give the ending a word.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a loaf of bread, drawn plain and appetising on the card. Name it, then let the real loaf take over — the card cannot be squished, and squishing is how this word gets remembered.

    Ask your child

    Watch the hands at the handover: squeeze first or bite first, and does the word or a sound arrive with either? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if soft is your favourite kind of word."

    What your child can say or do

    A squish and a giggle, the word "bread" or "beh" attempted at the counter, the card matched to the toast with a satisfied tap, or bread demanded at every meal for a week by name — fixation is fluency practice, not fussiness.

    Out in the real world

    Bread runs through the week: the bakery counter, the toast smell in the morning, sandwiches at the park. Every sighting is one word away from a rehearsal — and this word gets a lot of sightings.

    Try it together

    Bakery game: set out card bread, real bread and a teddy, and let your toddler hand out pieces — "bread for teddy, bread for you". Giving and naming is a complete language workout disguised as lunch.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word arrive with the texture rather than from across the room, and did your toddler get one honest squish? The hands remember what the ears are offered.

    Parent tips

    Name it at the giving, not on a loop — one word per handover keeps the kitchen calm. If your toddler lives on bread this month, good: repeated words are strong words, and the menu always widens eventually.

    Staying safe

    Toast crusts and chewy bites need watching teeth and a seated toddler — soft is the rule for new chewers. Keep the card out of the toaster’s neighbourhood; paper and heat have nothing to say to each other.

    This lesson pairs with the Bread flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    Egg — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The egg card is the set’s shape lesson hiding in a food: small, oval and at the table most mornings. This lesson names it at breakfast and lets the shape do its quiet work.

    What is this?

    An egg is a small oval food with a shell, famous at breakfast and endlessly useful in a kitchen. The card shows a simple egg; the real one — boiled, scrambled or still in its shell — gives the word its weight and its shape.

    What does it mean?

    Shape rides along with object words for free: every "egg" is also a quiet lesson in oval. Toddlers sort the world by shape and routine before colour or category, and the egg is one of the cleanest shapes on the menu.

    What does the child need to know?

    Show the card beside a real egg — in the shell is best — and let the two be compared: same word, same shape. One word, one clear form, one daily rehearsal: that is the entire method, and it is enough.

    Why this matters

    Eggs are breakfast regulars, which gives the word a reliable daily stage. The clear oval also seeds early sorting — round things, oval things, eggy things — the quiet beginnings of the maths your toddler will meet in a few years.

    What it teaches

    Object vocabulary with shape attached, matching picture to object, breakfast routine words, and early visual sorting — round, oval, rolls nicely.

    Words to learn

    eggovalshellbreakfastcrackround

    Say this to your child

    “"Egg! A little egg, smooth and oval. Feel it — cool and smooth in your hand. Crack — the shell opens, the egg comes out. Cook, cook, and now we eat the egg. Yum, yum, little oval egg."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at breakfast with a real egg in its shell beside it: "Egg. This is an egg — same as that."
    2. Let your toddler hold the real egg with your hand cupped under theirs: one word at the handover — "egg" — and the shape in the palm.
    3. Tap-tap-crack it into the pan if you are cooking, and name the moment: "Crack! The egg opens." The word for the sound is free vocabulary.
    4. Point at the card’s egg, then the shell pieces: same word, before and after. Toddlers love a before-and-after.
    5. Serve it and finish the scene: "Eat the egg. Yum." The oval’s journey ends at the fork, and the story has a shape too.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a simple egg, small and oval on the card — the plainest picture in the set. Say that, then hand over the real thing: the card shows the shape, and the shell supplies the coolness, the weight and the crack.

    Ask your child

    Watch the hold: do the fingers explore the curve, does the egg get rolled along the tray, does the word arrive at breakfast unprompted? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if you are storing the oval for later."

    What your child can say or do

    An egg carried to the card for a matching tap, "egg" or "eh-guh" attempted at the pan, both hands rolling the shell pieces, or the word offered at the fridge door a day early — naming across days is the word taking root.

    Out in the real world

    Eggs appear all over: the box in the fridge, the boiling pan, egg on toast, the scrambled spoonful. Each visit is a rehearsal — one word, one shape, and the oval gets around.

    Try it together

    Oval hunt: after the card, find oval things together — the egg, a stone, a lemon. A two-item hunt is plenty at this age; the shape is the treasure.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the card meet a real egg this week, and did the shape get said out loud once? Word plus shape is the double payload; either alone is half a lesson.

    Parent tips

    One word per egg — "egg", not egg-shell-oval-chicken; the extras leak in over years, not days. If the crack startles your toddler, show the cracking again slowly; surprise repeated on purpose becomes interest.

    Staying safe

    Raw egg stays a grown-up object — hand over boiled eggs in the shell only, wash hands after shell play, and keep the card clear of the pan’s splash radius. Breakfast stays seated: ovals roll, and so do toddlers who chase them.

    This lesson pairs with the Egg flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    Cup — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Cup is an old friend from the earlier sets, and the reunion is the lesson: your toddler meets a word they half-know in a new place, and the word gets stronger for it.

    What is this?

    A cup is the drinking vessel your toddler has been mastering for months — held, tipped, thrown, retrieved. The card shows the family cup; the word has history now, and this card lets your toddler show you how much of it they own.

    What does it mean?

    A word that returns across sets is not wasted breath — returning words are the spine of early vocabulary. Meeting "cup" again in a new place teaches your toddler that words are stable: the same name for the same thing, wherever it appears.

    What does the child need to know?

    Let your toddler lead: hand over the card and wait. Many will "read" it from memory — a word, a sound, a point — and that is reading in its first form. Confirm warmly and add the sip: "Cup. Drink."

    Why this matters

    Recognising a known word in a new place is comprehension deepening — your toddler is learning that pictures, objects and sounds all file under one name. That filing system is where every later word will be stored.

    What it teaches

    Vocabulary consolidation, picture-to-object matching, recall and "reading" from memory, and drinking skill — the word and the expertise growing together.

    Words to learn

    cupholddrinktipemptymore

    Say this to your child

    “"Cup! You know this one — your cup. Here is the picture cup, and here is your real cup, waiting. Hold it, tip it, sip, sip. Drink from your cup, my clever one. All gone — empty! The cup goes back for next time."”

    Step by step

    1. Hand your toddler the card before you say anything, and see what comes back unprompted — a word, a point at the kitchen, a beeline for the real cup.
    2. Confirm whatever arrives: "Yes! Cup. Your cup." The confirmation is the lesson; the leading was the test you never had to run.
    3. Bring the real cup beside the card: "Cup and cup. Same word." Say the rule once, lightly, and let the matching finish the argument.
    4. Name the action at the next sip: "Drink from your cup." The word now covers thing and action — a two-for-one.
    5. Finish with the empty cup held high — "all gone!" — the ending that always gets a grin.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is the family cup, plain and familiar — a picture your toddler has effectively met before, in sets and in kitchens. Say the word and let the recognition show; the response is the content of this lesson.

    Ask your child

    Watch the reunion: does a word come before you offer one, does the card get carried to the real cup? Wonder aloud: "I wonder how long you have known this word better than you can say it."

    What your child can say or do

    The word "cup", "kah" or "duh" delivered on sight, the card matched to the real cup with a proud double-tap, both hands lifting the real cup for a solo drink, or the card handed to you as a drink order — recall plus request is the full circuit.

    Out in the real world

    Cups are everywhere: the bathroom beaker, the picnic cup, the one at grandma’s. Every one is a replay of a word your toddler already owns — and owned words get stronger every time they work.

    Try it together

    Cup stack and name: two plastic cups, stack them, knock them, name each knock "cup!". Simple, physical, repeatable — and the word gets said by both of you until the game dissolves into giggles.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did your toddler get the first turn at the word, and did you confirm rather than correct? Leading and confirming keep the recall loop warm; quizzing switches it off.

    Parent tips

    Do not quiz — "what is this?" pressure turns recall into performance. Offer the silence and let the word volunteer itself. If your toddler brings you the card as an order, fill it: symbols that get results get used again.

    Staying safe

    Keep drinks upright and within reach but never poised above heads — a tipped cup from height is a cold surprise. And keep the card dry: once it has met actual milk, it retires to the memory shelf with honour.

    This lesson pairs with the Cup flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS: FOOD & HOME · AGES 12–18 MONTHS

    Spoon — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Spoon has been on the team since the first solids, and by now your toddler wields it with something between skill and weather. This card names the tool and turns finding it into the game.

    What is this?

    A spoon is the scooping tool of every meal — held, banged, loaded, inverted. The card shows a trusty spoon; the drawer supplies dozens. At 12–18 months the spoon is also a project: your toddler is learning to get food to mouth with one.

    What does it mean?

    The spoon card doubles as a find-it game: say the word, let your toddler’s eyes and feet hunt for the real one, and the finding completes the loop. Finding a named thing is comprehension made visible — the word went in, the object came out.

    What does the child need to know?

    Run the hunt gently: say "spoon", open the drawer cupboard together, and let the discovery be theirs. Name it at the find — "Spoon! You found it" — and again at the giving. Two landings, no quiz.

    Why this matters

    Hunt games turn vocabulary into little quests, made for the busiest bodies in the house. Each found spoon is proof that words point at real things, which is the whole deal language offers — signed and delivered.

    What it teaches

    Comprehension through finding, object permanence out in the open, spoon skill (scooping, wrist rotation), and mealtime vocabulary that carries real wants.

    Words to learn

    spoonscoopfindmoretapdip

    Say this to your child

    “"Spoon! A trusty spoon. Scoop, lift, in it goes. Now, where would a spoon hide — in the drawer! There it is. You found the spoon. Here is your spoon for dinner: scoop, scoop, yum. The spoon works, and so do you."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at a calm moment: "Spoon. This is a spoon — you eat with it."
    2. Mime the scoop in the air: scoop, lift, to the mouth — the action picture your toddler is already studying at every meal.
    3. Say "spoon" and hunt the kitchen drawer together; let your toddler find the real one and name it at the find: "Spoon! You found it."
    4. Hand the spoon over at the next meal and name the giving: "Your spoon." Then let the practice happen in peace.
    5. Keep one spoon in the toy box for scooping and dumping games between meals — the word gets off-duty rehearsals too.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a spoon, drawn plain and trusty — one tool, no clutter. Name it, then watch the live version: the grip, the upside-down loading, the determined stabs. The card shows the tool, your toddler the work-in-progress.

    Ask your child

    Watch the hunt: does the search start before you finish the word, does the right drawer get opened? Wonder aloud: "I wonder how many spoons you think the world holds."

    What your child can say or do

    A dash to the drawer at the word, the real spoon presented with a "doo!" of triumph, the spoon banged on a pot lid as drum practice, or a first loaded scoop delivered all the way to the mouth — skill and word, both under construction.

    Out in the real world

    Spoons live all over: the drawer, the bowl, the toy kitchen, the pot-lid drum kit. Every sighting takes one word, and the meal itself is the word’s daily dress rehearsal.

    Try it together

    Scoop station: a bowl of dry oats, two spoons and two cups. Scooping, dumping, refilling — the spoon word rides on a game your toddler would play anyway.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did one find-it hunt happen this week, and did the mealtime practice stay uninterrupted? The game teaches the word; the peace teaches the skill.

    Parent tips

    Let the messy self-feeding run — the spoon years are sloppy on purpose, and hovering corrections sour both dinner and the word. Name the tool at handovers, not on a loop; the spoon does the talking.

    Staying safe

    Choose spoons with soft tips for gums, skip sharp-edged serving spoons, and stay close while your toddler practises standing up with one. The card stays out of the porridge — paper does not survive the breakfast shift.

    This lesson pairs with the Spoon flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS: FOOD & HOME · AGES 12–18 MONTHS

    Shoe — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    Every outing has a costume change, and the doormat is the stage. This card names the shoe at the exact moment feet become outdoor feet.

    What is this?

    A shoe is the foot’s going-out gear, and at 12–18 months it is a daily costume change: shoes on to leave, shoes off at home. The card shows a shoe; the doormat supplies the stage, twice a day or more.

    What does it mean?

    Shoe is a routine word with feelings attached: shoes mean outings, and outings mean the park, the ducks, the world. Words loaded with anticipation get said early — the front door is a motivation machine.

    What does the child need to know?

    Say the word as each shoe lands on its foot: "One shoe... two shoes!" The chant makes it rhythmic, and the counting sneaks in free. Then let your toddler’s own "shoe" at the doormat — if it comes — be celebrated like the headline it is.

    Why this matters

    Routine words have perfect timing, built-in rehearsal and real consequences: shoes on means going out. Your toddler is not just learning a noun; they are learning that words live on transitions, which is where most of a day’s drama happens.

    What it teaches

    Routine vocabulary at transitions, one-two counting through dressing, walking skill (new shoes, new ground), and spontaneous naming at meaningful moments.

    Words to learn

    shoefootonoffwalkout

    Say this to your child

    “"Shoe! One shoe, two shoes — on they go. Shoe on the left foot, shoe on the right foot. Stand up, little one — shoes mean outside! Off we go, walk, walk, walk. And at home: shoes off, toes free, all done."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card in the morning, shoes already in view: "Shoe. Shoes on — we are going out."
    2. Say the word as each shoe lands on its foot: "One shoe... two shoes!" Slow, chanted, unhurried.
    3. Point at the card’s shoe, then the wearing ones: "Shoe and shoe." The match completes itself.
    4. At the doormat, say the word once more — "shoes!" — and let the outing begin; the word now carries the whole adventure.
    5. Coming home, run it in reverse: "Shoes off!" Endings of routines are their own lessons, and this one happens at your door.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a shoe, plain and clear on the card — the going-out kind, small and familiar. Say that, then look down: the live shoes are being worn by the actual critic, and the fitting is the show.

    Ask your child

    Watch the doormat across the week: does the word, a point or a lifted foot arrive at the shoes? Wonder aloud: "I wonder if the shoes or the outing is the real attraction."

    What your child can say or do

    "Shoe!" announced at the doormat, one foot offered grandly for fitting, the card carried to the shoe rack for matching, or both shoes carried around the house as luggage — the word travelling with the object is the milestone.

    Out in the real world

    Shoes run through every day: on to leave, off to arrive, the tiny pairs at the shop, the big pairs by your bed. Each changeover is a showing of this card.

    Try it together

    Shoe parade: line up three pairs at the door, name each pair, and let your toddler choose the day’s pair by handing one over. Choosing by naming is decision-making with vocabulary attached.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word land at a real transition this week, and did you cheer any doormat attempt? Transitions are this word’s home ground; the cheering is the amplifier.

    Parent tips

    Dressing battles and vocabulary lessons are separate events — if the shoes are a fight today, name them and move on. The word does not need the cooperation of the foot it describes.

    Staying safe

    Check the fit often — new walkers outgrow shoes in weeks — and slow the doormat changeover: loose laces, too-big shoes and rushing all trip new walkers. Keep the card in your hand until the feet are done.

    This lesson pairs with the Shoe flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS: FOOD & HOME · AGES 12–18 MONTHS

    Sock — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The sock card comes with two games built in: dressing and peek-a-boo. This lesson runs both — word at the foot, word at the hand-puppet — and lets the giggles do the gluing.

    What is this?

    A sock is the soft, stretchy foot-covering your toddler wears, pulls off and occasionally wears on a hand. The card shows a sock; your laundry pile supplies the population. Few words this age come with so much handling built in.

    What does it mean?

    Clothing words come round every day — sock, shoe, coat — and each rehearsal happens right on the changing mat. The sock also doubles as a toy: stretched over a hand it becomes a puppet, and puppet games make words unforgettable.

    What does the child need to know?

    Name it at the moment of use: "Sock. On goes the sock." Then the bonus game — sock over your hand, "peek!" — and the same word covers both. One word, two games, double the glue.

    Why this matters

    Dressing-table words are among the most-repeated a toddler hears, which makes them high-probability early words. The sock’s stretchiness also gives busy fingers a workout — pulling, stretching, poking are hand-skills in disguise.

    What it teaches

    Clothing vocabulary through routine, fine motor work (pulling, stretching, poking), peek-a-boo as object-permanence practice, and word learning through repeated games.

    Words to learn

    socktoepullstretchpeeksoft

    Say this to your child

    “"Sock! A soft little sock. On goes the sock — toes hidden! Pull, pull — off comes the sock. And look: the sock is a puppet now. Peek-a-boo, says the sock. One sock, two games, and the best giggles in the laundry."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card at dressing time, sock in hand: "Sock. On goes the sock."
    2. Name it as it lands: "Sock on! Toes hidden." Then enjoy the foot wiggle that follows — every toddler answers a covered foot with a kick.
    3. Play the pull-off: let your toddler tug the sock free — "off comes the sock!" — and name the ending they engineered.
    4. Stretch the sock over your hand: "Peek-a-boo! The sock says peek." Same word, second game, guaranteed laugh.
    5. Offer the sock to your toddler’s hand for a puppet round of their own, and let the game run until it dissolves — that dissolution is the finish line, not a failure.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a sock, soft and stretchy-looking, plain on the card. Name it, then bring out the live one: the card cannot be pulled over a hand, and the hand-puppet version is where this word gets its laugh track.

    Ask your child

    Watch the two games: does the pull-off or the peek earn the bigger laugh, and does the word get tried at either? Wonder aloud: "I wonder whether you think the sock is clothing or theatre." The honest answer is both.

    What your child can say or do

    A sock yanked off and held up like a trophy, "sah" or "sok" attempted at the change table, the puppet sock patted or kissed, or a sock worn proudly on the hand all morning — at this age, wearing it wrong is still wearing the word.

    Out in the real world

    Socks are everywhere: the laundry basket, the drawer, the odd one under the sofa, the pairs on everybody else’s feet. Naming them on sight turns housework into a language walk.

    Try it together

    Sock matching: two pairs of baby socks, mixed up — find the twins together and name each match "sock, sock!". Matching play is the 12–18-month specialty, and laundry made it first.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the naming happen during a real dressing moment, and did the puppet game happen at least once? Routine and play — the two ways this word gets glue.

    Parent tips

    Follow the fun: if the puppet game beats the dressing lesson, the puppet wins — the word is the same in both. Single socks lost to the sofa monster are fine; the word does not need the pair.

    Staying safe

    Keep socks out of mouth range at play — the stretchy kind compacts alarmingly — and check the puppet sock for loose threads. The card stays clear of the changing table; changing tables and paper have a feud going.

    This lesson pairs with the Sock flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).

    LEARNING PATH LESSON · FIRST WORDS: FOOD & HOME · AGES 12–18 MONTHS

    Chair — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

    The set closes with its largest exhibit: furniture. Naming the chair hands your toddler a word for the seat they already rule, three meals a day.

    What is this?

    A chair is the seat your toddler climbs at every meal — their throne, their height advantage, their place at the table. The card shows a sturdy chair; the word closes the set because by now it has handed over words for meals, clothes and seating — a fair slice of daily life.

    What does it mean?

    Furniture words mark a scale change: the chair is bigger than your toddler and stays put. Naming big fixed things teaches that words also cover the scenery of life, not just the grabbable props.

    What does the child need to know?

    Name it at the climb: "Chair. Up you go." Word at the climb, climb at the word — the two arrive together, and neither forgets the other. Stay close; climbing is the main sport of the era.

    Why this matters

    The chair carries the meal ritual — sitting, eating, finished, down — so it is a sequence hub as much as an object. Words at hubs get used constantly, which is why chair often outlasts fancier words.

    What it teaches

    Furniture vocabulary, climbing and sitting coordination, sequence words around meals (up, sit, eat, finished, down), and the pride of naming the biggest thing in the room.

    Words to learn

    chairsitclimbseatupdown

    Say this to your child

    “"Chair! A big sturdy chair — your chair. Up you climb, sit yourself down. The chair holds you while you eat, the chair waits for you at breakfast. All finished — down you come, carefully. Thank you, chair. What a good seat."”

    Step by step

    1. Show the card just before a meal, chair in sight: "Chair. This is your chair."
    2. Point at the card’s chair, then the real one: "Chair and chair." Same word, one picture, one throne.
    3. Say the word at the climb — "chair! up!" — with your hand hovering at your toddler’s back, close enough to be the safety rail.
    4. Once seated, run the meal’s little sequence lightly: "Sit... eat... yum." The chair is the stage and the sequence is the play.
    5. Finish the meal with the descent: "All finished — down you come." The word for the ending is the word for the whole ritual’s close.

    Look closer at the picture

    The artwork is a sturdy chair, drawn plain and upright — the largest object on any card in this set. Name it, then gesture at the room: the real chair holds your toddler right now, which makes this the easiest live match in the collection.

    Ask your child

    Watch the climb: does a leg lift at the word, does the pointing finger find the real chair from the card? Wonder aloud: "I wonder when the seat and the seat’s name became one thing to you."

    What your child can say or do

    "Chair!" or "tair" called at the kitchen seat, the climb attempted with the word as its soundtrack, the card carried over and propped on the chair seat — matching at scale — or a proud bottom delivered to the named seat: naming, matching and doing, the full trio.

    Out in the real world

    Chairs are everywhere: the high chair, the sofa’s end, the little seat at the play table, every chair in every café. The set closes with a word your toddler will rehearse for years without ever needing the card again.

    Try it together

    Musical sit: tap a beat, stop it, and both of you find a seat — the sofa, the floor cushion, the chair. Naming each seat as it is found turns a party game into furniture vocabulary.

    Understanding check

    Parent self-check: did the word ride a real climb, and did the meal sequence get its quiet narration — up, sit, eat, down? Hubs and sequences are where this age files its best words.

    Parent tips

    This card finishes the set — say so, and make the finish feel like a finish: cards away, "all done!", a smile. Sets that end deliberately get reopened sooner. The chair word will keep working long after the cards are tucked away.

    Staying safe

    Climbing is the era’s main sport: stay within an arm for every chair ascent, check the chair’s stability before it becomes a gym, and keep the card off the seat — a sitting toddler and a paper throne disagree about weight limits.

    This lesson pairs with the Chair flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to First Words: Food & Home (Toddler 1).
